column4: The garden owners swear to cut their crop in the morning, expecting a later yield from what they have kept growing. This is a direct harvest-time scene against the section’s palm whose fruit remains until the final picking.
While they sleep, an affliction from their Lord passes over the garden overnight. The verse supplies the intervening delay that turns the planned morning harvest into a lost one.
The garden is found as though cut down or blackened. This reverses the section’s image of fruit remaining on the tree through the harvest season.
The owners call one another at daybreak. This is the morning threshold at which the planned harvest is to begin.
They urge one another to go early to their crop if they mean to reap it. The verse makes the harvest timing explicit.
They reach the garden early, determined to keep the poor from it. This continues the planned harvest and shows that its expected yield is already treated as secured.
When they see the garden, they think they have lost their way. Their first expectation of a harvest is reversed by the ruined crop.
They realize instead that they have been deprived. This names the outcome of a crop they expected to gather later.
After the garden is lost, its owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better, خيرا منها. The verse gives the section’s خ ي ر sense a concrete later compensation after an earlier loss.
The verse says the punishment of the Hereafter is greater than this punishment. It sets the garden’s present loss beside a later consequence.

The verse pictures tall date palms with clustered fruit. It gives the section’s dictionary image of a palm carrying its crop a concrete Quranic scene; the previous and following verses supply rain and provision.
The verse calls the produce provision for servants and says dead land is revived by it, “thus the emergence.” Its own contribution connects yielded provision to the later return.
God says He has decreed death among people and cannot be outdone. This makes the first life’s endpoint appointed, alongside the section’s later creation and outcome.
The following verse says God can change people’s forms and bring them into an unknown form. It completes the preceding decree of death with the later transformation.
All on earth is described as perishing. This marks the finite end of the first, earthly span against what remains.
The face of the Lord, possessor of majesty and honor, is said to remain. It supplies the enduring side of the perishing/remaining boundary.
Those before are made to taste disgrace in worldly life, while the punishment of the Hereafter is greater. The later outcome outweighs the earlier one in the opposite, punitive direction.

Those who emigrated after being wronged are promised a good place in this world, while the reward of the Hereafter is greater. It is a specific present/later valuation tied to a real change of circumstance.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a heavy day. This is an explicit preference for the near term over the later one, contrary to the section’s valuation.
The verse says people love the immediate life. It isolates the first side of the contrast completed by the next verse.
The verse says they leave the Hereafter. Together with verse 20, it names the contrary choice to the section’s better-later weighing.
At the end, a person regrets not having sent deeds ahead for “my life.” The verse makes the earlier opportunity and later reckoning one concrete sequence.

The verse asks who seeks the reward of this world, then says with God is the reward of both this world and the Hereafter. It places both temporal rewards under one owner, as in the section’s first/last pair.

The verse says each soul dies only by God’s permission at a written term, then distinguishes those seeking the world’s reward from those seeking the Hereafter’s. It joins appointed timing to a choice between the two rewards.
After the believers’ prayer, God gives them the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter. This is a concrete instance of a later reward completing an earlier trial.

The verse asks whether it should tell the God-fearing of something better than worldly desires, then names gardens and God’s pleasure. It turns the section’s choice of the better of two matters into a direct world/Hereafter comparison.

The verse says people may dislike something that is good for them and love something that is bad, while God knows and they do not. It supplies a specific reversal in how an outcome is judged, related to the section’s better choice.

The captives are told that if God knows good in their hearts, He will give them better than what was taken from them and forgive them. This is a concrete later compensation for an earlier taking, using the section’s better-choice root.

After Yusuf’s story of reversal and establishment, the verse says the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and fear God. It is another explicit statement of the section’s later-abode valuation.

The preceding surah ends by promising that the one who gives seeking his Lord’s face will surely be satisfied, ولَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ. This closely matches the section’s affirmed future gift ending in satisfaction.
The verse says that with hardship comes ease. It offers a specific before/after parallel to the section’s comparison of the later state with the earlier one.
The repeated assurance says again that with hardship comes ease. Its repetition makes the later relief certain, like the section’s emphatic promise of what is to come.
The oath names the morning as it brightens. This is a precise light-increasing threshold parallel to the section’s post-sunrise sequence.
The verse says the warning is for whoever wishes to advance or lag behind. This directly names the section’s first/later relation as movement forward or backward, with the warning as its boundary.
Every soul is then said to be held in pledge for what it earned. This supplies the later accounting that follows the advance/lag choice in verse 37.
The oath names the night as it departs. This gives the dark side of the transition completed by the next verse’s breathing morning.
The oath names the morning as it breathes. That image matches the section’s light increasing at a threshold after sunrise.
Each community has an appointed term, and when it comes it cannot be delayed or advanced. This is a direct statement of a fixed endpoint for the section’s deferred-time image.
Each community has a term; when it arrives, it cannot be delayed or advanced even an hour. The verse repeats the section’s fixed-endpoint relation with an explicit measure of time.
No community precedes its term or delays it. This states the boundary around postponement in the section’s timed promise.
The people are called to worship and forgiveness, and God will defer them to a specified term; once it comes, it cannot be delayed. It joins a promised respite to its fixed end.
The call to seek forgiveness is followed by a promise of good enjoyment until an appointed term and a reward for every possessor of bounty. This is provision granted over a bounded future interval.
The punishment is delayed until a countable term, and the deniers ask what is holding it back. The verse makes postponement itself a challenge before the promised outcome.
The messengers say God calls people to seek forgiveness and will defer them to an appointed term. It is a direct instance of respite with a later deadline.
God does not overlook wrongdoers; He only postpones them to a day when eyes stare. The verse makes the deferred reckoning explicit.

People ask for punishment to be hastened, but God will not fail His promise; a day with Him is like a thousand years by their count. It links delay to a radically different measure of the promised time.
The verse says that if God hastened evil for people as they hasten good, their term would already have been concluded. It makes the contrast between human haste and deferred divine timing explicit.
The deniers are warned not to mistake their reprieve for good; the respite increases their burden before humiliating punishment. This is a boundary on reading delay as a guaranteed benefit.
God is said to create people from clay and then set a term, with another specified term known to Him. This ties the beginning of human life to its appointed later limit.

God promises many gains, hastens one for the believers, and holds another gain they could not yet reach within His power. It is a specific promised benefit divided between an immediate portion and a later one.

God confirms the Messenger’s earlier vision and promises entry into the Sacred Mosque, with a near victory placed before it. The verse joins an earlier sign to its later fulfillment for the same addressee.
Yusuf welcomes his parents and family into Egypt in safety just before naming the fulfillment of his former dream. This is the reunion that precedes the delayed dream’s completion in verse 100.
Moses says his Lord knows who will have the good outcome of the Home. This uses the section’s endpoint/result idea to frame the final outcome beyond a present dispute.
